title: Maine’s Senator Collins Bets on Bringing Home the Bacon to Win Reelection
summary: What’s better than bacon? For Maine, it might be “bringing home the bacon”—a funny way of saying a politician gets federal money for their state. Republican Senator Susan Collins is really good at it, and she’s hoping it will help her win another term. Her opponent, Democrat Graham Platner, says the whole system is unfair to working people. Collins has been in the Senate for a long time, and now she’s the chair of the powerful Appropriations Committee. That means she helps decide how the government spends money. She’s already used her position to get cash for a breakwater dock in Eastport, a town with just over 1,000 people. Her first campaign ad bragged about it! She also helped fund community colleges, stop cuts to science research, and even fight a hungry caterpillar that eats Maine’s trees. Collins says her seniority is a “once in a century” opportunity for Maine. But Platner’s team argues that while Collins brings home small projects, many Mainers are still struggling because of bigger policies she supports. His campaign manager said, “Every time Sen. Collins leverages a little bit of an earmark to build a bridge or a road, that just does not make up for the fact that Mainers right now are hemorrhaging money.” Collins also spoke out against tariffs that could hurt a paper mill on the Canadian border. She wants voters to imagine life without her in Congress. A professor said that message works well with independent voters, but this year might be tougher because many people are unhappy with Republicans nationally. It’s a race that could decide which party controls the Senate!
why_it_matters: This shows how elections can become a debate about whether a long‑serving politician’s small local wins matter more than the bigger economic problems people face because of national policies.

keywords.explanation: Money that comes from the national government, not from a state or city.
A powerful group in the U.S. Senate that decides how the government will spend its money.
A special amount of money that a politician adds to a big spending bill for a specific project in their own state or district.
Extra taxes that a country puts on goods coming from other countries, which can make those goods more expensive.
The longer a politician has served, the more experience and power they usually get in Congress.
A strong word that means losing a lot of something very quickly — in this article, losing money fast.

background_read: Susan Collins has served as a U.S. Senator from Maine since 1997 and is known for sometimes working with both parties.
The Senate Appropriations Committee is one of the most powerful committees in Congress because it decides where trillions of dollars in federal money go each year.
An earmark is when a member of Congress adds a specific spending request for a project in their home state, like a dock or a road, into a much larger spending bill.
Article_Structure: WHO: Republican Senator Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Graham Platner.
WHAT: Collins is campaigning on her seniority and ability to direct federal money to small projects in Maine, while Platner argues that bigger policies are making life harder for ordinary people.
WHERE: The state of Maine, with examples like a dock in Eastport and a paper mill near the Canadian border.
WHY: Collins wants to keep her Senate seat by showing she brings real benefits home, and the race could decide which party controls the entire Senate.

perspectives.description: Many Mainers appreciate Collins because she uses her experience to fund small‑town projects like docks and to fight tariffs that threaten local paper mills.
They argue that a few small projects do not make up for the fact that many Mainers are struggling with high costs and policies she helped support.

Analysts say that bringing federal money home has often been a winning strategy, especially with independent voters, but this year a national wave of unhappiness with Republicans could make it much harder for her.
